text:
Many older adults wake up from surgery confused, frightened or “not themselves,” and families are often told it’s just age. In this video, we explain what postoperative delirium is, why the brain is more sensitive to anesthesia, pain medicine and hospital stays after 65, and why the quiet, sleepy kind of delirium is so often missed.
We count down five common mistakes people make before and after surgery. They include saying “I’m fine” when you aren’t, bringing an incomplete medication and supplement list, leaving glasses and hearing aids at home, going without water longer than needed, and spending all your questions on general vs. spinal anesthesia. Then we walk you through The Clear Mind Plan, a simple step-by-step routine for the weeks before surgery, the hospital days and the first two weeks at home. A version of this routine, with family members helping each day, cut delirium from about 1 in 5 patients to fewer than 3 in 100.
If you or someone you love has a surgery coming up, this lesson will help you prepare your body, your bag and your questions for the anesthesia team.


Research referenced in this video:
Neuman MD et al. REGAIN Trial, spinal vs. general anesthesia for hip surgery. New England Journal of Medicine, 2021.
Moller JT et al. ISPOCD1, long-term postoperative cognitive dysfunction in the elderly. The Lancet, 1998.
Makary MA et al. Frailty as a predictor of surgical outcomes in older patients. Journal of the American College of Surgeons, 2010 (Johns Hopkins).
Wang YY et al. Tailored, family-involved Hospital Elder Life Program and postoperative delirium. JAMA Internal Medicine, 2020.
American Society of Anesthesiologists. Practice Guidelines for Preoperative Fasting, 2023 update.
American Society of Anesthesiologists. Herbal and Dietary Supplements and Anesthesia.
Multi-society clinical guidance on GLP-1 receptor agonists before procedures, 2024.
American Geriatrics Society. Postoperative Delirium in Older Adults: Best Practice Statement, 2015.
American Geriatrics Society. Beers Criteria, 2023 update.

Medical disclaimer: This video is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to your own doctor or surgical team before changing any medication, supplement or fasting instruction.

If this lesson helped you, subscribe to Senior Health Board for clear, research-based health lessons for people over 60. Tell us in the comments: L, Q or S?

What Happens When You Start Eating Peanut Butter Every Day After 60 | Doctor Explains

Is peanut butter good for you after 60? One spoonful of peanut butter a day can help your heart, your muscles and your blood sugar, or it can quietly work against all three. In this lesson, we follow one spoonful of peanut butter through the body of someone over 60: the mouth, the stomach, blood sugar, muscles and the arteries. You’ll learn what eating peanut butter every day really does for seniors, and why the way you eat it matters as much as the peanut butter itself.
Large studies link eating peanuts to fewer heart attacks and strokes, but peanut butter didn’t show the same protection. We explain why, and how to choose the healthiest peanut butter for seniors. You’ll see how to read the label, which ingredients to avoid (added sugar, salt and hydrogenated oil), why “reduced fat peanut butter spread” is often the worse choice, and how much peanut butter per day is right after 60. We also cover peanut butter and blood sugar, peanut butter for diabetes and prediabetes, protein for muscle loss (sarcopenia) in older adults, and safety tips for dry mouth, swallowing problems, kidney disease and nighttime heartburn.
At the end, you’ll get the Flat Spoon Plan: six simple steps to eat peanut butter the healthy way after 60, starting this week.



Research referenced in this video:
Reis CE et al. British Journal of Nutrition, 2013: peanuts and peanut butter at breakfast, fullness hormone PYY and the second meal blood sugar effect
Alper CM & Mattes RD. International Journal of Obesity, 2002: daily peanut intake and body weight
Jiang R et al. JAMA, 2002: nut and peanut butter consumption and type 2 diabetes risk in 83,818 women
Paddon-Jones D & Rasmussen BB. Current Opinion in Clinical Nutrition and Metabolic Care, 2009: protein per meal and muscle loss in older adults
National Institutes of Health, Office of Dietary Supplements: magnesium intake in older adults
Guasch-Ferré M et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology, 2017: nut and peanut intake and cardiovascular disease in more than 210,000 adults
Ikehara S et al. Stroke, 2021: peanut intake and stroke risk in 74,793 Japanese adults
Luu HN et al. JAMA Internal Medicine, 2015: nut and peanut intake and mortality in more than 200,000 adults in the US and Shanghai
American Heart Association: replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fats
US Food and Drug Administration: standard of identity for peanut butter (21 CFR 164.150)
National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research: medicines and dry mouth
This video is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to your own doctor before changing your diet, especially if you have kidney disease, swallowing difficulties, diabetes or a peanut allergy.

How do you usually eat your peanut butter? Tell us in the comments. If this lesson helped you, subscribe to Senior Health Board and share it with someone you love who’s over 60.

5 Medical Checkups I’d NEVER Get After 70 (#1 Is the One Everyone Gets) — Doctor Explains

After 70, some of the most common medical checkups can do more harm than good, especially when you feel perfectly fine. In this video, we look at 5 routine medical tests seniors are often offered at their yearly physical, at a pharmacy or at a church health screening: the whole-body MRI or CT scan, the carotid artery ultrasound, the PSA test for prostate cancer, the urine test without symptoms, and the routine TSH thyroid test that can lead to a thyroid pill for life.
You’ll learn how one small finding on a test can start a chain of follow-up scans, biopsies, antibiotics and new medications, why false alarms become more common after 70, and what the research says about overdiagnosis and overtreatment in older adults. We also cover thyroid medication and bone fracture risk, antibiotics for bacteria in the urine, and PSA screening and biopsy risks after 70.
At the end, you’ll get The Pause Plan, a simple routine to use before your next checkup, along with the questions to ask your doctor about any screening test, so you can decide which tests still make sense at your age.


Research referenced in this video:
Ganguli et al., Cascades of Care After Incidental Findings, JAMA Network Open (2019)
Royce et al., Cancer Screening in Older Adults With Limited Life Expectancy, JAMA Internal Medicine (2014)
Whole-Body MRI Screening in Asymptomatic Adults, Cancer Imaging (2020)
American College of Radiology, Statement on Screening Total Body MRI (2023)
Warren et al., Adverse Events After Outpatient Colonoscopy in the Medicare Population, Annals of Internal Medicine (2009)
US Preventive Services Task Force, Screening for Asymptomatic Carotid Artery Stenosis, JAMA (2021)
US Preventive Services Task Force, Screening for Prostate Cancer, JAMA (2018)
US Preventive Services Task Force, Screening for Colorectal Cancer, JAMA (2021)
Nicolle, Asymptomatic Bacteriuria review (2016)
Infectious Diseases Society of America, Guideline for Asymptomatic Bacteriuria, Clinical Infectious Diseases (2019)
Stott et al., TRUST Trial: Thyroid Hormone Therapy for Older Adults With Subclinical Hypothyroidism, New England Journal of Medicine (2017)
Turner et al., Levothyroxine Dose and Risk of Fractures in Older Adults, BMJ (2011)

Disclaimer: This video is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to your own doctor before changing any test, treatment or medication.

Which of these 5 tests surprised you most? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for more health lessons for people over 60.

second kind is what this whole lesson is

The advertisements are everywhere,

This is the smoke alarm pointed at the

In an older body, a single scan will

says a great deal. And a 2020 review in

Because when researchers put 12 studies
and 6,214
scans of healthy people side by side, 95

If you have a specific worry, a symptom,

particular cancer, the better path is to
ask your doctor which single targeted
test fits that concern, while keeping up

recommended at your age.
The next test shows up in places you'd
never expect to find a medical exam,
like a church hall or a pharmacy parking
lot.
Test number four is the carotid
ultrasound, a scan of the big arteries
in your neck. And the mistake is signing
up for one when you've never had any
signs of a stroke.
These screenings are often sold in
packages at community centers and
churches, where a technician runs a
probe along your neck for a few minutes.
The carotid arteries carry blood up to
your brain. And like garden hoses used

on their inside walls with age. And the
ultrasound isn't perfect at telling a
small narrowing from a significant one.
A positive screen usually leads to a CT
or MR scan of the arteries and a visit

talk of surgery or a stent, both of

meant to prevent.

whose whole job is to decide which

at this question again and published its

good and they gave it a D grade, which

Gene, 73, a retired city bus mechanic
from Pennsylvania, did the $49 scan.
He was told he had moderate narrowing on

He ended up on the same blood pressure

arteries. If you feel fine, the most
protective thing you can do for your

brother, or a father over 70, it's just
as much your business. Test number three
is the PSA blood test for prostate
cancer and the mistake is continuing to
get it every year after 70. PSA is a
protein the prostate releases into the
blood and it rises with an enlarged
prostate, with infection, and sometimes
with cancer. So a high number alone
can't tell you which. Most prostate
cancers found in men over 70 grow so
slowly that many men live out their
lives without the cancer ever causing a
problem. But once a number comes back
high, the usual next step is a biopsy
where a needle takes small samples of
the prostate. A biopsy can cause
bleeding and infection, and if a slow
cancer is found, the conversation often
moves towards surgery or radiation,
which can leave a man with leaking urine
or erection problems for the rest of his
life. In 2018, that same task force
looked at PSA testing and gave it a D
grade for men age 70 and older. And
their reasoning makes sense once you
hear it because at this age, false
alarms are more common, biopsies cause
more problems, and treatment side
effects hit harder. Even so, the habit
is hard to break. And back in 2014, a
University of North Carolina team looked
at survey answers for more than 27,000
Americans over 65 and found that more
than half of the older men whose health
was already fragile, men who weren't
expected to live another 9 years, were
still getting PSA tests, which shows how
easily this simple blood test stays on
the lab slip year after year without
anyone asking whether it still helps.
Bill, 76, a retired insurance agent from
Missouri, had his PSA checked at every
annual physical. When the number crept
up a couple of points, he was sent for a
biopsy. And 2 days later, he was back in
the hospital with a fever and an
infection that kept him there for 3
nights. The biopsy showed a small,
slow-growing cancer that his urologist
recommended simply watching, which is
roughly where he had started.
If you're a man over 70 and you feel
fine, it's worth asking your doctor
whether PSA still belongs on your yearly
blood work. Trouble passing urine, blood
in it, or new bone pain are symptoms.
And then testing is the right move.
The next test is the simplest one on
this list, which is the reason so few
people ever think to question it. Test
number two is the urine test, and the
mistake is having your urine checked for
bacteria when you have no burning, no
fever, and no new urgency. Then being
treated with antibiotics because
something grew in the lab. As we get
older, the bladder often carries
bacteria without any infection at all.
Doctors call this asymptomatic
bacteriuria, which means bacteria in the
urine without symptoms, and it's far
more common than people think. Because
in 2016, Dr. Lindsay Nicolle at the
University of Manitoba pulled together
the research and found that by age 80,
about one in five healthy women living
at home will have bacteria show up in a
urine test while feeling perfectly well.
A positive result usually brings an
antibiotic, and antibiotics in older
people bring their own risks from
stomach upset and diarrhea to a serious
bowel infection called C. diff. In 2019,
the Infectious Diseases Society of
America updated its guidelines and said
plainly that older adults with some
frailty living at home and people in
nursing homes should not be tested or
treated for these bacteria when they
have no symptoms because the evidence
shows the antibiotics cause real harm.
The same experts also found no good
evidence that confusion, falls, or
strong smelling urine are caused by a
positive culture on its own, and that
matters because once the urine gets the
blame, the real cause can slip right
past everyone. Dolores, 82, a widow from
Tucson, got muddled one hot July
afternoon, and at urgent care, a urine
test came back positive, and she went
home with a week of antibiotics. Nobody
asked how much water she'd had that day,
and by day four, the antibiotic had
given her diarrhea that left her so weak
she slipped in the hallway and badly
bruised her hip. Her confusion had come
from dehydration in the desert heat, and
a few glasses of water would probably
have cleared it. A urine test makes good
sense when you have burning, a fever,
pain in your side, or a a new urgency.
If you or someone you love seems
confused, it's worth asking whether
something else could be behind it, such
as too little water, a new medicine, or
a poor night's sleep before anyone
reaches for an antibiotic. If you're
still with me, type the word f i n in
the comments, because protecting that
feeling of being fine is what this whole
lesson is about.
Number one keeps its hold on people the
longest, sometimes for decades, and it
starts with one number on an ordinary
blood panel. Test number one, and the
one I guess more of you have been
through than any other, is the TSH
thyroid blood test. And the mistake is
getting it routinely while you feel
perfectly well, and then being started
on a thyroid pill for life because the
number came back slightly high. TSH
stands for thyroid-stimulating hormone,
the thermostat signal your brain sends
to the thyroid gland in your neck,
telling it to turn the body's heat up or
down. With age, that signal naturally
drifts a little higher. And when TSH
sits above the range while the thyroid
hormone itself is normal, doctors call
it subclinical hypothyroidism, an
underactive thyroid on paper only.
Between 8 and 18% of people over 65 have
this pattern. And the usual response is
a daily pill called levothyroxine. The
biggest test of this idea was a trial
called TRUST, run by researchers at the
University of Glasgow and published in
the New England Journal of Medicine in
2017
And the way they set it up was very
fair. They took 737 people age 65 and
older whose thyroid number stayed a
little high when it was checked twice,
gave half of them the real pill, and the
other half a dummy pill that looked
exactly the same, and nobody knew who
was getting which. After a whole year,
the two groups felt the same, with the
same tiredness and the same thyroid
symptoms, which means the pill wasn't
doing anything people could actually
feel. And the researchers said plainly
it shouldn't be handed out routinely to
older people with this mild pattern. The
other side of the story came from the
University of Toronto in 2011 when
researchers looked at 213,511
people age 70 and older who were taking
this pill and found that those on the
higher doses had about three and a half
times the risk of breaking a bone
compared with those on low doses.
Carol, 74, a retired church organist
from Georgia, was started on a thyroid
pill 9 years ago after a routine panel
showed a TSH of 6 even though she felt
fine. She never noticed a difference.
The prescription refilled itself every 3
months and nobody lowered the dose as
she got older and lighter. Last winter,
she stepped off a curb outside the post
office and broke her wrist and when her
new doctor finally rechecked her levels,
her thyroid was running too high.
A pill, once started, rarely gets
questioned again, which is why this one
lasts for years. If you're already on a
thyroid pill, please don't stop it on
your own and talk to your doctor before
changing any medication. But, it's very
reasonable to ask whether your dose
still fits your age and if a new
borderline number appears, to ask for a
recheck before anything is started. So,
let's turn all of this into something
you can use and I call it the pause plan
because the whole idea is one calm pause
between being offered a test and saying
yes to it. And it takes about 25 minutes
a year to prepare. The first part
happens about a week before your yearly
checkup. Sit down at the kitchen table
with a pen and a sheet of paper and
spend 15 minutes writing down every test
you remember having in the last 2 years.
Next to each one, write F if you had it
while feeling fine because it was
routine and S if you had it because of a
symptom. Most people are surprised by
how long the F side turns out to be. The
second part is the age check, which
takes another 10 minutes. For each test
on the F side, look at whether it still
fits your age according to independent
guidelines, which the US
Preventive Services Task Force posts for
free online.
As a starting point, the task force
recommends against PSA screening for men
70 and older and against carotid artery
screening for people without symptoms
and says colon cancer screening between
76 and 85 should be an individual
decision based on your health and past
screening. While the radiologist's own
professional group doesn't recommend
whole body scans for healthy people,
circle anything on your list that falls
into one of those groups and those
circles become your talking points.
The third part happens in the exam room
and it's the pause itself. When a test
is offered and you feel fine, you can
say something as simple as "Before we do
that one, I'd like to understand what we
do with the result." and then listen. A
good doctor will welcome that. If the
answer is vague along the lines of "It's
just routine." that's your cue for the
questions I'll give you in a moment. If
you're finding this plan useful, type
plan in the comments so I know to put
more lessons like this one on the board.
The fourth part is a habit I call repeat
before treat. If a borderline number
comes back, whether it's a slightly high
TSH, a small bump in PSA, or a urine
culture with bacteria but no symptoms,
you can ask whether it makes sense to
repeat the test in a few weeks or months
before starting any treatment. Numbers
like TSH bounce around after a cold or a
bad week, which is why the TRUST
researchers only counted people whose
number stayed high on a second check.
The fifth part is a yearly medication
bag check. Once a year, put every pill
bottle you take, prescription and
over-the-counter, into a bag and bring
it to your appointment or your
pharmacist and ask them to look at each
one with your current age and weight in
mind.
This is the step that would have caught
Carol's thyroid dose years earlier and
any change that comes out of it is made
with your doctor, never on your own.
To get started, in the next 7 days do
the kitchen table list and mark your F's
and S's.
Within 14 days, call your doctor's
office and ask which routine tests are
planned for your next visit. And within
30 days, at your appointment, use the
pause. Bring your circled list and your
medication bag and ask your questions.
There are times when a test is exactly
the right thing and no plan should slow
you down. If your face droops on one
side, an arm or leg suddenly goes weak,
your speech becomes slurred, or you feel
chest pain or pressure spreading to your
arm or jaw, call 911 right away. Blood
in your urine or stool, burning with a
fever, a new lump, weight loss you can't
explain, or a cough that won't go away
all deserve a prompt visit to your
doctor. Because in every one of those
cases, testing is how you get answers.
At your next checkup, a good opening
sentence is, "I'm feeling well, and
before we do any routine tests this
year, I'd like to talk about which ones
still make sense at my age." A useful
first question after that is what the
two of you would actually do if a
particular test came back abnormal, and
what those next steps would mean for
someone your age. After that, you might
ask whether an independent group like
the US Preventive Services Task Force
recommends the test for a person your
age with no symptoms. And finally, if a
number comes back borderline, whether it
can be repeated before any treatment
begins. Tell me in the comments which of
these five tests surprised you most.
Just its number from one to five,
because your answers help me decide what
to put on the board next. Please send
this to someone you love who's over 60,
especially the one who agrees to every
test without a second thought. Because
one pause could spare them a very long
year. Tap subscribe so you don't miss
the next lesson where we look at the
shower and bathroom habits that send
more people over 60 to the emergency
room than almost any other room in the
house. This is Senior Health Board.
Feeling fine is worth protecting, and
I'll see you in the next lesson.

The #1 Old-Fashioned Food for Tired Blood After 60

Always tired after 60? Feeling worn out by the afternoon, even after a full night’s sleep? In this video, we look at blackstrap molasses, the old-fashioned black syrup that American grandmothers kept in the pantry and took by the spoonful as a tonic for “tired blood.” Blackstrap molasses is made from the third boiling of sugarcane, and one tablespoon contains iron, calcium, magnesium and potassium, minerals that many seniors and adults over 60 don’t get enough of.
We count down five benefits of blackstrap molasses for seniors: more antioxidants than honey or white sugar, minerals for bone health and osteoporosis prevention, a gentler effect on blood sugar and insulin, potassium for heart health and blood pressure, and iron for fatigue and low energy linked to iron deficiency anemia. You’ll also hear the true story of the 1950 bestseller “Look Younger, Live Longer” and why the FDA seized copies of it in 1951.
Most importantly, you’ll learn the common morning habit that blocks the iron in molasses, how to take blackstrap molasses the right way with lemon and vitamin C, a simple five-minute molasses oatmeal breakfast recipe, and who should be careful, including people with diabetes, kidney disease or hemochromatosis.


Research referenced in this video:
Phillips, Carlsen & Blomhoff, Journal of the American Dietetic Association (2009): antioxidant content of sugar and natural sweeteners, Virginia Tech
Ellis et al., European Journal of Nutrition (2016): sugarcane molasses concentrate and insulin response, Australia
